title: Practical empathy
content:
I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe.

And that’s okay.

In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen.

Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and our approach than anyone else. We have a noise in our head, a narrative and a point of view we’ve spent our whole lives creating. It’s naive to believe that anyone else is completely in sync with us.

And so, our only opportunity is to go where they are, not to demand that they come to us.

Practical empathy isn’t primarily an act of kindness (though it’s an essential component of kindness.) Instead, it’s a direct and straightforward path from here to there. It’s how we create action, learning and change.

Marketing is the simple and brave act of going to where someone else might be, and helping them get to where they hope to go.

title: Is Science a Mirror, a Game, or a Conversation?
content:
Science is a slippery concept. It’s tough to fit into a neat box with fixed edges. It is digging up artifacts in the desert, peering at microbes through powerful instruments, theorizing about the expansion of the universe, writing code for new technology, retracting a paper riddled with errors, admitting you were wrong, starting over, making accidental discoveries, experimenting on yourself with psychedelic drugs. It is also exploring genetic code, curing disease, connecting people through instant global communication, and engineering weapons of mass destruction. It is demystifying rainbows. It is riddled with bias, but it is the most rigorous system humans have for discovering things about the world.

But what separates science from non-science exactly and who decides? Recently, University of California, Berkeley, psychologist Marina Dubova and Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu decided to try to take on the elusive task of answering these questions—of defining science.

**Read more:**[**“The Thrill of Science in 2042”**](https://nautil.us/the-thrill-of-science-in-2042-1270684)

Is science like holding up a mirror to ourselves, reading the book of nature, or is it a game of competition, strategy, or chance? Metaphors, they decided, could be wrestled into service for their cause. They chose 18 metaphors that have historically been used to describe science and then surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public about how accurate they found the metaphors. They published their [results](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/13/11/260933/484137/Everyone-knows-what-science-is-until-you) in _Royal Society Open Science_.

I spoke with Dubova about why the distinction between science and non-science matters, which metaphors appeal to her most, why we need “radically exploratory” approaches to scientific discovery, and what AI will do to creativity in the sciences.

**You write in your new paper that science has a demarcation problem, that it’s been very difficult to solve the question of what precisely separates sciences like physics and biology from non-sciences or even pseudosciences like astrology. Why is that?**

It’s very hard to solve the demarcation problem because science is such a versatile activity and that’s what our paper also shows. As a cognitive scientist who studies concepts, I know that all human concepts are fuzzy and versatile. Even when you talk about very commonly used concepts like birds. What is a bird? Nobody can give you a precise definition. Even though we coordinate around what we call bird and what we don’t call a bird, if we actually study the inner structure of these concepts in individual minds, there’s a lot of diversity. That’s why trying to define anything, to put strict boundaries around concepts, becomes problematic.

It’s a big issue with science specifically because that’s a concept where we do need to draw the line sometimes. And the diversity of understandings has run up against attempts to propose just one or a few criteria, for example, like falsification, to distinguish science from non-science. There are all these other ways in which scientists can conduct themselves that still lead to successful discoveries historically.

**You say science needs to draw the line sometimes. Why?**

There are many practical senses in which we do want to distinguish between scientific evidence-based advice for the public, versus non-scientific advice. But sometimes it’s really hard. Just thinking about scientific advice as coming from the community of scientists doesn’t appeal as neatly to people. We want to see beyond that: What exactly is it about scientists that allows them to offer this advice that is more legitimate? We want to help people trust scientific advice as compared to other kinds of information we might encounter across the internet.

**Your primary finding was that scientists disagree about science more than the public does. What do you think is going on there?**

Scientists are the people who are engaging in science in versatile ways, so you see more variability in the way they describe it than in people who are potentially non-expert. That’s something we might expect from any domain of expertise. It’s not necessarily unique to science.

The reason we were interested in this question is because I have training in science, and my colleague Ella has training in science. During our training in science, we were taught all these amazing methods: how you can measure this, measure that, operate this specific piece of technology. But in our experience, it was never a point of discussion to talk about our understanding of science.

That felt like a paradox. In science, we often disagree about very specific aspects of scientific policy and methods. In psychology and cognitive science, there is a big debate about pre-registration and replication. Is it worth replicating someone else’s study or is it better if I do my own new study? People disagree a lot about this.

When we disagree with each other, we might think, “Oh, this person just must not understand how important replication is.” But in my opinion, it actually goes much further. We may have very different conceptions of what science actually is. These kinds of cognitive attitudes about science may play a big role in scientist disagreements, but we never zoom all the way out. We often focus on specific disagreements and stay there. That’s why we wanted to know what scientists think about science.

**You also found that the public has a more idealized version of what science is today than the scientists. There are a couple of reasons why you thought that might be, including possibly your study sample, but I was still really surprised by this, given the strong anti-science bent that has dominated politics at least in the United States lately. Is there any way in which that kind of idealism about science could be helpful?**

We are still thinking about it, and this study is just the first step. There’s so much more to be done, and our small sample of the public is nowhere near to capturing the diverse conceptions of science that people have.

You would think, “Oh, trust in science is declining and everybody has started hating science.” Politically we can see that happening and that was kind of my belief. But according to recent meta-analyses across different countries, it turns out that most people still trust science a lot. Maybe not medical advice from scientists, or some very specific things, but basically people still report that they think science is very valuable for society.

The conclusion from that literature seems to be that the people who don’t trust science are a noticeable minority. They speak very loudly. We hear from them all the time. That’s why we think that trust in science is declining.

Our study is consistent with that. Individuals seem to be very optimistic about science. But it is a double-edged sword. It’s great to see that a lot of people think science is so valuable. But I wonder—and we don’t have any data yet to support this—whether these kinds of heightened expectations might raise suspicion about scientific advice that so often comes with a lot of caveats. If the public is expecting a definitive finalized conclusion, they might reject pieces of advice that come with all kinds of uncertainty.

That’s the main feature of scientific advice: It’s going to be updated, it’s going to include all kinds of caveats. Because that’s what science is about—being able to revise and capture the uncertainty. And that’s what scientists in our study sample were speaking about: The uncertainty and all the other aspects that come into the act of trying to evaluate scientific evidence.

That is potentially the next stage of this research for us, to look at whether idealism about science can make it more difficult to evaluate real scientific claims. How does it affect communication between the public and the scientists? When we do science communication, there’s always this assumption of alignment between the speaker and the receiver. But if we have completely different expectations, we might run into problems.

**You use metaphors to try to approximate a definition of science in the study. Can you explain how you chose the metaphors that you used and tell me whether there a few that you personally like best or are the most true to what science is?**

We mostly collected these metaphors through reviewing the literature in philosophy and history of science, and by looking at how scientists talk about themselves. My co-author Qiawen Liu and I did this together. Of course, this is in no way comprehensive. In the future, something we really want to do is scrape these metaphors from public discourse about science, also. But this is just the first step.

There are a few metaphors that I love the most. My favorite one is about how it is a kind of “haptic engagement with reality.” That comes from this philosophical conception of “haptic realism.” Basically, the idea is that the scientific process consists of us interacting with the world in such a way that when we’re measuring it, we may inadvertently affect the phenomenon itself. It’s always about the relationship between the observer, or the scientist, and the phenomena. We’re just trying to explore it in this tactile way.

The reason I like this metaphor is that in our data, we found that a lot of the historical conceptions of science are visual. We’re looking at the world and we’re taking pictures, or we’re building images of the world, or we’re looking with a flashlight or mirroring reality. But a couple of philosophers of science, [Mazviita Chirimuuta](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fg%2F11b7qd6bms&q=Mazviita+Chirimuuta), and Hasok Chang, emphasize the many ways in which science is not visual or well captured by this visual metaphor, because we are not just passive observers. We are actively choosing what to measure. We’re interacting with people who we are trying to describe. In many ways, we’re affecting the world around us. And that’s a very important aspect about science that needs to be highlighted more. It’s something I’ve been learning through the philosophical work. It was not the way I originally thought about science.

A related conception is that science is an iterative dialogue with nature. It’s not just me observing passively what’s going on there. It’s me actively choosing what to query about and then receiving some kind of information based on that query. I think these are very important aspects of science that often get neglected in visual frameworks.

**You wrote a speculative fiction piece for****_Nautilus_****earlier this year. You write about a not-so-distant future when science has shifted from this very rote process into a more creative one that you call “radically exploratory science.” I wonder if you feel that science is already in a rut and needs to shift toward the radically exploratory?**

In my opinion, yes. I love science. I think science is the best thing that has happened to society and I love my colleague scientists. But one part that I love about science is that we also are very open to rethinking what science is and what science is about and noticing when some of our methods are not working as effectively in helping us learn about the world. My own personal conception of science made me realize how important this radically exploratory part is and how at the moment it is not very consistent with how we think about science.

Often when we think about science, it’s something premeditated. You need to know why you’re doing a specific study. There’s so much emphasis on rational premeditation and rational intention. When we propose grants, we need to already have some data that shows we’re going to see what we’re going to see. If we are proposing to do this specific experiment, we need to have a really good rationale. Is it helping us with this theory or this other question?

What was surprising to me, coming from this more cognitive view about science, is that it seems like that’s exactly the wrong way to think about many aspects of science. If we look at any cognitive systems that learn about the world, they start with a lot of exploration. That’s how you get to learn things that you don’t expect to see.

**What influence do you think AI will have on how we understand science and the scientific method? Can it support greater creativity in science or will it do the opposite?**

I think it can do both. AI by itself is not necessarily one thing or another. It’s based on how we deploy it. I’m both very excited about the advances AI has for science, but I’m also very worried alongside many of my colleagues about how AI is currently being deployed and how it can potentially remove any kind of exploration.

Basically, a lot of people are reporting this possibility that AI will decrease the amount of exploration we’re already doing in science. Some literature on this topic that I really appreciate talks about the danger of a scientific monoculture.

Laura Messeri and Molly Crockett have been at the forefront of advocating that AI may turn science into a monoculture. The idea is that each AI model obviously comes with its own biases. It’s not one objective view from nowhere. I’ve heard that kind of worry being raised even now when it comes to AI being used for mathematical discovery where mathematical discovery is equated to just being able to prove things. If you ask mathematicians what they think they’re doing, it’s much more than that. Are we going to be able to capture all these diverse conceptualizations and diverse understandings of what we are even doing, when we are trying to scale up science with these models? That’s something to really keep in mind. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: When Parasites Have Parasites
content:
While it sounds like something from a sci-fi movie, “hyperparasitism” is a legit scientific term for when a parasite infects another parasite (as if one parasite wasn’t trouble enough). Although apparently widespread, the phenomenon is little studied. A [recent paper](http://dx.doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2026.1772) published in _Proceedings of the Royal Society B_ detailed the relationship between the fungi that cause powdery mildew in plants and another fungus (_Ampelomyces_ spp.) that piggybacks on it.

The powdery mildew fungi (family Erysiphaceae) are infamous in the agricultural industry, since they’re obligate parasites—i.e., they can only survive on living plant tissue—of many crops, including wheat, grapes, and soybeans. In all, they attack 10,000 species of flowering plants. When you add _Ampelomyces_ to the equation in a “parasite-on-parasite system,” however, crops have a better chance at survival.

**Read more: “**[**Parasites Can Also Be Friends**](https://nautil.us/parasites-can-also-be-friends-359523)**”**

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” explained senior study author Michael Bradshaw, an entomologist and plant pathologist at North Carolina State University, in a [press release](https://news.ncsu.edu/2026/11/even-parasites-have-parasites/).

Powdery mildews can’t be cultured, and so, Bradshaw and coauthors screened 609 samples of dried powdery mildews from herbarium specimens originally collected from 28 countries over the last 150 years. Hyperparasites can’t easily be detected with the naked eye, but DNA sequencing, followed by microscopy, revealed the presence of _Ampelomyces_ parasites on 40 specimens. 671 more _Ampelomyces_ gene sequences were found in the genetic repository GenBank.

This hyperparasite turns out to be much more common than previously thought, with about seven percent of all powdery mildews examined in the study carrying _Ampelomyces._ It was also more diverse than expected, with five distinct genera encompassing 47 different strains, including some possible new species. “Collectively, these results highlight the evolutionary and ecological complexity of the _Ampelomyces_-powdery mildew system,” wrote the study authors.

There’s not just a fungus among us—there are fungi on fungi. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Animals Defying the Climate Odds at the Top of the World
content:
On my first afternoon in Arctic Svalbard in June 2024, two filmmakers in my guesthouse tell me that reindeer are just outside. I have flown halfway around the world to witness these reindeer, and here they are, under our window. I grab my binoculars and boots, walking into a sudden spring snowstorm to see a small herd of reindeer munching on the tundra.

These are not the majestic flying reindeer of Christmas cards. They are stocky, goat-sized, roly-poly survivors—evolutionary success stories that sparked the central questions of my journey: Why would reindeer come to this inhospitable archipelago where glaciers still cover more than 60 percent of the land? How did they transform their bodies and behaviors to thrive in one of Earth’s harshest environments? And as climate change warms Svalbard faster than almost anywhere on Earth, what hope do they have?

We often tell a simple story about Arctic wildlife: as the climate warms, cold-adapted animals disappear. Svalbard’s reindeer suggest a more hopeful and more complicated one. They are not passive victims of climate change. They explore new foods, shift their movements, pass knowledge to their young, and change their bodies over generations. They appear to have agency. And if that’s true, it changes what we might do to help them.

I spent a month on the archipelago, part of it aboard the three-masted _Antigua_ with the Arctic Circle Residency, a floating gathering of artists, scientists, filmmakers, and journalists reflecting on climate and environmental futures. Before and after the residency, I stayed at Mary-Ann’s Polarrig, a funky guesthouse decorated with walrus penises and old mining photographs, where Polish glaciologists waited for the waves to calm and the daughter of a Chukchi reindeer herder staffed the front desk.

At first glance, Svalbard seems like a poor bet for any land mammal. The soil is thin and starved of nutrients, and the sparse browse can’t feed many mouths. In the brief summer that punctuates the winter darkness, reindeer roam through High Arctic valleys in small groups, grazing on grasses, forbs, and tiny willow shrubs in the few ice-free lowlands. Winter is particularly challenging. Polar bears and whales can dive beneath the pack ice to find food, but when the darkness comes, reindeer must crater through the snow for mosses and lichens.

Svalbard’s food web is pared down to the basics. Little auks fertilize the tundra with their droppings, reindeer eat the resulting vegetation, and when they die, Arctic foxes feast on the carcasses. With few predators, weather becomes the main variable shaping populations, which turns the archipelago into a natural laboratory for understanding climate impacts elsewhere.

Isolated for millennia, Svalbard reindeer face a climate paradox. Warming temperatures extend summer growing seasons, allowing reindeer to pack on more calories before winter. But although they double their fat during summer and subsist on those reserves for part of winter, eventually they must forage. If winter rain falls and freezes, ice can form a shell three feet thick over lichen. Reindeer hooves, evolved for cratering through snow, cannot pierce this frozen armor. Many starve. In poor years with winter rain, adult females who survive until spring weigh only around 103 pounds—less than some dogs. In winters without rain, they can weigh 126 pounds.

Reindeer have always survived the occasional rainy winter, often by miscarrying a pregnancy to save the mother. But two rainy winters in a row make survival precarious, and the effects ripple outward to voles, ptarmigan, and foxes.

A TOUGH DIET: Reindeer are well-adapted to snow and cold, but winter rains present a challenge, for they cannot easily crater through the ice to food, which is usually lichen. _Credit: Nancy Langston, original linocut print, 2024_

On my third day, I climbed Sarkofagan, one of the mountains ringing Longyearbyen, Svalbard’s main settlement. Polar bears roam, so you must always hike with an armed guide. Mine was Maria, an Italian geologist finishing a master’s thesis on permafrost.

At the summit cairn, Maria pointed across the fjord to ancient shorelines etched nearly 260 feet above today’s coast, relics of an Arctic shaped by the chaotic transition between the most recent expansion of the ice and our current epoch, the Holocene. Around ten thousand years ago, vast ice sheets retreated, meltwater flooded the oceans, and ice-dammed lakes failed catastrophically, sending walls of water across the landscape. The Polish scientists waiting out the waves at my guesthouse have documented 134 glacial lake drainage events.

I asked Maria why reindeer might come to such a volatile place, and she shrugged. Rocks, she told me, change for predictable reasons, which is why she studies them. Mammals rarely follow laws, scientific or political.

What we do know comes from genetics and archaeology. Svalbard’s reindeer originated in what’s now Russia, and perhaps seven thousand years ago, some individuals crossed the 35 miles of the Kara Strait to Novaya Zemlya, the anvil-shaped archipelago curving into the Arctic Ocean. Some later trekked about 220 miles over pack ice to Franz Josef Land. When glaciers advanced thirteen hundred years ago, most of the reindeer died out, but a few migrated again, trekking roughly 160 miles across sea ice to Svalbard, where the Gulf Stream makes the climate slightly milder.

But could reindeer really cross that distance on pack ice? It seemed impossible, until in 1912, a hunter shot a Svalbard reindeer with an ivory gull’s foot tied to its left antler. This individual had walked over from Novaya Zemlya, where Indigenous Nenets herders marked their reindeer that particular way. The decorated reindeer proved reindeer could make the long crossing on pack ice. But it doesn’t explain why they made that journey.

Picture a reindeer in Russia thousands of years ago, on her annual migration north to the Kara Sea. She reaches the coast in May, her body heavy with a calf after seven and a half months of pregnancy. Behind her lie raging rivers swollen with snowmelt, their banks lined with the bodies of other females who drowned as they tried to swim across. Pack ice groans against the coastline, shifting in the spring Arctic winds. Cows who survived the initial journey browse the thawing tundra, pulling up tufts of grass. Males remain distant; females have kept their antlers throughout the winter to drive them away during calving season. Then, for reasons known only to her, one cow steps onto the pack ice. No certainty of food awaits her. Perhaps an island shimmers on the Kara Sea’s horizon, and something in her imagines, “That might be a good place to birth my calf.”

When I had met with reindeer ecologist Sam Dwinnell in a bustling Longyearbyen café the afternoon I arrived, I asked her as well: Why did reindeer come to Svalbard? Like Maria, she considered the question carefully before shrugging. Knowing a reindeer’s mind is all but impossible. Yet I can’t stop wondering: What compelled that reindeer to leave familiar tundra to cross hundreds of miles of treacherous ice? Why journey northward until you reached the fragile edge of an Arctic archipelago still largely glaciated? What prompted enough of her herd to follow that they reproduced and established themselves on the edge of a glacial wilderness?

Trees and people may provide part of the answer. About 10,300 years ago, extensive environmental changes rippled across northern Eurasia and forests expanded. Reindeer faced a dilemma: Adapt to forest life or flee to open tundra landscapes beyond the reach of trees and the human hunters who used forests for cover. Some populations adapted to become forest reindeer, herded by humans. But others apparently moved northward across the pack ice, seeking open tundra habitats.

Reindeer across the globe have been extraordinarily resilient to past climate changes. At the end of the last glacial maximum, as the glaciers retreated, reindeer chased the melting ice north, exploring new environments and expanding their range across the circumpolar north. Unlike most other Pleistocene megafauna, reindeer populations expanded in size at the end of the Pleistocene. Mobility was central to reindeer’s post-Pleistocene resilience.

Reindeer made human life across the Arctic possible as climates changed in the Late Pleistocene, letting people thrive in otherwise uninhabitable ecosystems. People followed the reindeer north in a warming world, and a striking diversity of human–reindeer relationships developed. But on Svalbard, no humans followed the reindeer. Archaeologists have searched for decades without finding a single trace of reindeer people—or other reindeer predators—so for millennia the reindeer evolved in the absence of predation.

Without predation, Svalbard reindeer rapidly developed new adaptations to a cold climate. Annual migrations shrank to a few miles, less than the average American commute. Reindeer’s physical form changed as well as their behaviors. Long legs and speed were less important than conservation of energy, and their bodies became rounder and capable of storing more fat, allowing them to double their weight during the brief summer months. Even their digestive systems transformed, with enlarged rumens that could process a wider variety of the tough plants growing at the edge of glaciers.

ARCTIC BEHEMOTH: A bowhead whale surfaced beneath the Antigua in the pack ice off Svalbard. _Credit: Nancy Langston, original linocut print, 2024_

Those adaptations would be tested when European ships appeared on the horizon. Whalers arrived in the early 1600s, and crews needed fresh meat, so hunters were sent into the valleys to shoot calving reindeer, the first systematic predation pressure on Svalbard herds.

On the _Antigua_, we sailed north toward the pack ice, retracing the journeys of whalers. At four in the morning, the engines changed their sound, and when I dressed and went on deck, my compass read 80°20′ N. Pack ice surrounded us. A few hours later, I was painting on deck when Alex, one of the artists, shouted, “Bowhead whale!” We rushed to the railing. I’m not entirely sure I saw her, only a shadow sliding beneath the ice, but knowing she swam under our boat felt like a gift. She could be two hundred years old, a witness to transformations that reshaped this archipelago long before any of us were born, and her ancestors’ songs once tied the Arctic together before whaling emptied the waters along Svalbard’s coast.

Bowheads are the only baleen whale that spends its whole life in the Arctic. Like reindeer, they survived the warming at the end of the Ice Age by following habitat northward. The Dutch built an enormous shore station at Smeerensburg, “Blubber Town,” in 1619, hiring Basque harpooners to run it.

Our Zodiacs drifted across teal water that mirrored black rocks and blue-gray snowfields, and kittiwakes chattered on the icebergs, stark white against the darkening sky. Their grace filled me with joy: life persisting despite three centuries of extraction. Then we walked the beach on Danskøya, near the ruins, falling silent as we realized we were crossing a graveyard of whales and men. Our guide Lars pointed to a ring of red stones: blubber cement, the residue of kettles boiling over. Scraps of blubber were tossed in the fires to render the rest, so the whales fueled their own undoing.

By the end of the seventeenth century, over ten thousand whalers spent part of each year in Svalbard. The coastal bowhead population soon collapsed. Not all the whales died, however. Some seem to have learned from their relatives’ deaths, avoiding the fjords and swimming away from the coast, eventually settling in the northern ice where whalers couldn’t follow.

Later, from a cliff above a fjord, I watched little auks, birds no bigger than sparrows, stream overhead by the hundreds of thousands. They and the bowheads, it turns out, eat much the same food. Here is where the story takes an ecological twist I find hard to stop thinking about. A bowhead weighs five hundred thousand times more than a little auk, yet when the whales vanished from Svalbard’s coasts, the zooplankton they left behind fed a boom in little auks, with the northeast Atlantic population climbing by about 70 percent.

Little auks became ecosystem engineers, comparable to beavers in temperate zones. Where little auks congregate, their nutrient-rich guano creates lush patches of tundra that support reindeer. Those reindeer, in turn, modify the landscape further and provide carcasses that support Arctic foxes. Whaling’s devastation created unexpected ecological opportunities. This doesn’t justify the slaughter, but it does illustrate nature’s ability to reconfigure after disruption. It is an ecological paradox: a human action as devastating as commercial whaling ultimately helped sustain reindeer.

Whaling was only the first wave of European hunters. The Pomors, walrus hunters from Russia’s White Sea, arrived in the 1690s. They were the first Europeans to thrive through the polar night, and reindeer kept them alive: At one archaeological site, reindeer made up 68 percent of the bone fragments, against just 8 percent for walrus. They wore reindeer pelts, walked in boots of reindeer felt, and slept between reindeer furs.

The human dead of whaling and Pomor centuries lie all along the coast, in hand-built coffins lined with fabric, their heads cradled on pillows of cloth scraps stuffed with little auk feathers, buried as deep in the permafrost as their comrades could dig and weighted with cairns against the bears. It was as if the dead were to be kept warm in a world that was otherwise cold and uninviting.

ADAPTING TOGETHER: Reindeer have adapted to a warming climate on Svalbard by foraging onkelp that warming currents bring north. Polar bears are adapting by eating those reindeer, since their typical prey, seals, have moved further offshore. _Credit: Nancy Langston, original linocut print, 2025_

The next wave of hunters were fur trappers, who were seeking out polar bears, foxes, and walrus for European markets. Like the Pomors, they rarely sold reindeer hides, but they relied upon their meat for winter survival. One of them was Wanny Woldstad, whose cabin we visited beneath a bird cliff near Hornsund. In 1932, she talked her way onto a winter crew and returned for five seasons, killing seventy-seven polar bears and countless foxes. Multiplied across Svalbard’s coasts, these hunting pressures devastated reindeer. Yet reindeer were not simply victims. They carried accumulated knowledge about where to calve safely, which valleys sheltered them from storms, how to find plants under deep snow. As predation pressures increased, reindeer retreated to valleys and heights that human hunters couldn’t reach.

And then came coal. John Monroe Longyear, an American who studied at what was then the Michigan College of Mines, founded the Arctic Coal Company in 1906 and built a company town that still bears his name. To feed growing mining communities, managers hired hunters to systematically target the reindeer herd that survived—a cheaper protein source than imported provisions. Miners wanted meat every day, so seasonal hunting shifted to year-round pressure, leaving the animals no respite even during calving. Previous waves of human exploitation—whaling, Pomor hunting, and fur trapping—had stressed Svalbard’s reindeer population, but industrial coal mining delivered a devastating blow.

In 1596, reindeer occupied virtually all unglaciated lands across the archipelago, as fossilized antlers show. When hunting was finally banned in 1925, only four isolated populations remained. For five decades, reindeer recovery was excruciatingly slow. In 1978, scientists tried active translocation, bringing three males and nine females from near Longyearbyen to Brøggerhalvøya, where a former mine was turned into the world’s northernmost research station. Reindeer had been absent from this area for more than a century. The translocation essentially created a controlled experiment: How would these animals fare in suitable habitat with no competition and no predators?

Despite Arctic desert conditions, the reindeer population exploded to 360 individuals in fifteen years. But during the winter of 1993–94, it crashed to just 78 animals. The cause was twofold: systematic overgrazing of preferred plant species and an extreme weather event that brought rain instead of snow. The year after the population crash, the surviving reindeer began to disperse to neighboring areas, becoming the source for those we saw grazing across much of the northwest coast. Their grazing, trampling, and fertilization altered vegetation communities, shifting them from moss-dominated to grass-dominated tundra. But forage alone doesn’t determine reindeer density; history does as well. Areas where reindeer had been extirpated a century earlier still show lower reindeer densities than expected based on vegetation productivity alone, suggesting that the legacies of overhunting persist in the ecosystem.

Having survived waves of human exploitation, Svalbard’s reindeer now face a threat that doesn’t target individuals but reshapes whole habitats. When winter rains fall and ice seals over lichens, some reindeer starve. Others have begun annual migrations again, heading to the coast, where they now feed on kelp—another climate migrant brought north by warming currents. Reindeer are adapting to rapidly changing conditions—just as they did thousands of years ago when they first ventured to these islands. And in doing so, they’re providing food for another mammal that had been expected to become extinct on Svalbard but is instead thriving.

On our way to the pack ice, a crew member cried, “Polar bear!” We crowded the railing and watched a massive male lope down a snowfield, bath in the sea, then stroll unhurried across the cobbles. We weren’t the only ones watching. Six reindeer paused their grazing to track his route.

Polar bears had rarely hunted reindeer in the past, because seals were abundant along the coastal pack ice and a much more rewarding morsel for a hungry bear. But now the coastal ice is dwindling, so polar bears can’t easily hunt seals. Our guide Audun explained to us that even though many news reports suggested Svalbard polar bears were starving and close to extinction, most were not. Instead, they were hunting the reindeer who had begun venturing down to the beaches to eat kelp. Neither eating kelp nor hunting reindeer is a sign of desperation; both are innovative responses that animals craft through exploratory feeding. Individual reindeer who venture to beaches and sample kelp may pass this knowledge on to others, particularly their calves. Polar bears who figure out how to surprise a reindeer are observed by their cubs, who learn new techniques. Both Svalbard reindeer and polar bears defy the catastrophic narratives we often construct about climate change. Behavioral plasticity—the capacity to innovate and share knowledge—may prove critical to their survival.

Reindeer around the globe speak to us not of untouched primordial wilderness but instead of the complex historical relationships between humans and reindeer that still influence modern conservation. Svalbard is far from pristine. The ground beneath one’s boots is layered with Nazi weather stations, whale bones, collapsed Pomor fox traps, and tangled fishing nets. And yet every day we witnessed resilience: kittiwakes rising and falling on the wind, little auks streaming to their colonies, pooping all the way, creating the lush pastures where reindeer flourish.

Svalbard reindeer are neither climate victims waiting for rescue nor relics to be frozen in place. They are participants in an ongoing story of adaptation that began long before we arrived and may continue long after our climate crisis has become another layer in the geological record.

In a world of constant movement and change, survival depends less on rigid boundaries than on the ability to migrate, adapt, and build relationships across difference. That means giving the animals room to move and to settle somewhere new, and being the kind of partners who listen when they show us where they want to go. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Check Out the First Photos of the Poles of a Rod-Shaped Bacterium
content:
It looks like some kind of distant alien world, but it’s actually something much smaller and closer to home.

For the first time, scientists have been able to capture detailed images of the poles at the end of rod-shaped bacteria—with the breakthrough coming not from a new type of camera or scanner but from being able to keep the small microbes still and alive for long enough.

**Read more: “[‘Zombie Bacteria’ Might One Day Lurk in the Sewers](https://nautil.us/zombie-bacteria-might-one-day-lurk-in-the-sewers-1286253)”**

The process is detailed in [a new study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78975-y) published in _Nature Communications_, and it involved sticking _E. coli_ bacteria to glass via a substance called glutaraldehyde, which binds to proteins on the surface of bacteria. Crucially, the chemical keeps the bacteria alive, preserving their structure.

The pole of an E. coli bacteria. _Credit: University College London_

From there, they could be scanned using atomic force microscopy, a technique where a probe just a few nanometers wide taps along the cell to image it. The researchers compare it to a human finger reading braille.

Even with this new technique, the snapshot required patience. It took 20 minutes for the stickiness to take effect on the organisms, and 50 minutes to find some of the trapped bacteria standing upright.

It’s been a long journey to get here, too. Getting bacteria to stand up straight for a photo has proved elusive across many experiment types. It’s worthy quest, though, as a look at the poles provides important information about the parts of these tiny cells that are used for growth and defense.

“Imaging the poles of bacteria is like opening a view of the back of the moon,” study author Bart Hoogenboom explained in a [statement](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/nov/poles-bacteria-imaged-fine-detail-first-time). “We’re looking at something that no one else has seen before. The poles are where cells divide, and so, (they) contain critical information about this process. They may also be a particular target for antibiotics, with some bacteria-killing treatments preferring to attack this part of the cell.”

With some of the most dangerous pathogens on the planet becoming increasingly resistant to our best drugs, these photos could help develop more effective treatments that attack specific vulnerabilities in the “armor” of the bacteria. And now that they’ve found an imaging approach that works, the researchers say it could be adapted to work over longer timescales as well—capturing processes like successive cell divisions and biofilm formations.

All of which is to say, there are a lot of other microbe poles to image—and many more brand new sights to analyze. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
content:
An era-defining galaxy survey has released its final results. They don’t quite fit the leading theory of cosmology.

![Image 1: Photograph looking into the open dome for the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope around sunrise or sunset in the Andes Mountains.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/DES-cr.Dark-Energy-Survey_DOE_FNAL_DECam_CTIO_NOIRLab_NSF_AURA-Lede-scaled.webp)

The 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera is mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope on Cerro Tololo near La Serena, Chile.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/  
 DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

[J oshua Frieman](https://www.quantamagazine.org/joshua-frieman-finding-dark-energy-in-the-details-20140918/) remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers announced that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, said Frieman, now at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”

Within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

Now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared[findings based on its full dataset (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27221) of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” said [Simone Ferraro (opens a new tab)](https://sferraro.lbl.gov/), a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”

![Image 2: A man stands at the base of the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope beneath a dome open to the daytime sky.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Joshua-Frieman-cr.Brian-Nord-scaled.webp)

Joshua Frieman, a physicist at the University of Chicago, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Brian Nord

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro said.

## **Bigger and Faster Forever**

Experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

In previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

But new observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

Then came the bombshell 1998 findings that the expansion of the universe was not actually slowing down; it was ever so slightly speeding up. By the end of the year, the unknown stuff driving that acceleration had a name: dark energy. Frieman charged off to measure it.

In 1998, cosmologists were like detectives with a thin dossier. They had a blurry image of light from the early universe known as the [cosmic microwave background (CMB)](https://www.quantamagazine.org/how-ancient-light-reveals-the-universes-contents-20200128/). And they had observed several million galaxies, along with dozens of supernovas. Because light takes time to travel, these observations gave cosmologists snapshots of what the universe looked like at different moments over the past few billion years.

![Image 3: A mosaic of CCD sensors on the focal plane of the Dark Energy Camera reflect blue light in a room lit in red.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Camera-cr.DOE-FNAL-DECam-R.-Hahn-CTIO-NOIRLab-NSF-AURA-scaled.webp)

The Dark Energy Camera holds an array of charge-coupled devices, or CCDs, similar to the sensors in normal digital cameras but designed specifically for astronomy.

DOE/FNAL/DECam/R. Hahn/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

That was just enough data to show that the universe was experiencing an unexpected growth spurt. But to figure out exactly when it had started and how fast it was happening, Frieman and his colleagues would need to fatten their file. Their solution was DES.

DES began in 2003, with a handful of physicists at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory brainstorming what it would take to get a more comprehensive view of the cosmos. They went on to design and build the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera, the most powerful digital camera of its era, and install it on the 4-meter-wide Blanco telescope in the Chilean Andes. They then used it to conduct the Dark Energy Survey, which ran for 758 nights between 2013 and 2019. During this time, DES increased the number of recorded galaxies to hundreds of millions. DES was supposed to end in 2018, but the researchers extended it to make up for lousy observations due to clouds from a strong El Niño season.

Every couple of years the DES collaboration, which grew to include more than 400 scientists across seven countries, would analyze the data they had collected so far to see what it suggested about the history of our universe. Again and again, what they found was consistent with the theory that had coalesced after the 1998 supernova papers: The universe was about 30% matter (mostly an invisible and lethargically drifting “cold dark matter,” or CDM), and the remaining 70% of the universe was dark energy. Physicists noted that this energy acted like an unchanging property of the vacuum of space, referred to as “lambda.” The bigger space gets, the more of this vacuum energy there is, and the faster the cosmos expands. This theory of the universe became known as Lambda-CDM.

Then, in 2024, researchers from a next-generation experiment, DESI, combined the DES observations with a sharper image of the CMB and new observations of their own. They found that the Lambda-CDM theory no longer quite fit.

## **Broken Record**

Whereas DES uses one big camera in Chile, DESI at Kitt Peak in Arizona uses thousands of tiny eyes. Each can swivel to focus on a single galaxy. The individualized attention more precisely captures each galaxy’s motion.

This technology lets DESI see hidden cosmic structures. Due to the way that sound waves rippled through matter in the early universe, spherical shells of slightly dense matter formed. Over time, matter in these shells gathered into galaxies. Each shell is the same size, so by looking at how big or small it appears from Earth, scientists can tell how far away its galaxies are.

Combining the distances to the galaxies with other observations, the researchers can calculate how fast the universe has grown over the past 10 billion years or so (out of the 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang).

![Image 4: Reddish dust and gas, vaguely shaped like two dragons facing on another, against a background of stars.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Fighting-Dragons-Nebula-cr.Dark-Energy-Survey-DOE-FNAL-DECam-CTIO-NOIRLab-NSF-AURA-scaled.webp)

Young stars emitting stellar winds shaped the dust and gas of the Dragon nebula, captured here by the Dark Energy Camera, into a form that resembles a pair of fighting dragons.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/  
 DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

In 2024, the DESI collaboration dropped a [bombshell report](https://www.quantamagazine.org/dark-energy-may-be-weakening-major-astrophysics-study-finds-20240404/). When researchers added their shells to the existing dossier, they couldn’t get the Lambda-CDM model to fit all the data. What fit better was an exotic theory that replaced lambda, the constant vacuum energy, with a different form of energy that weakened over time. A year later, an analysis of more data [found the same thing](https://www.quantamagazine.org/is-dark-energy-getting-weaker-new-evidence-strengthens-the-case-20250319/).

In the meantime, the DES collaboration continued to analyze the galaxies they had photographed. Those researchers focused on building a different contribution to the dossier: a detailed record of a cosmic tug-of-war.

While gravity pulls matter — mostly dark matter — together, dark energy fights back, pushing matter apart. By measuring how much matter has clumped together in different eras, cosmologists can infer the strength of dark energy over time.

DES assesses this clumping using three methods, explained [Sujeong Lee (opens a new tab)](https://www.ohio.edu/directory/sujeong-lee), a physicist at Ohio University. First, DES measures how tightly galaxies of visible matter cluster together, which reveals how much dark matter floats around them. Second, it maps out visible matter in the foreground by looking for the ways it distorts light coming from galaxies in the background. And third, it maps out foreground dark matter in a similar way.

Each of these measurements involves comparing pair after pair of DES’s hundreds of millions of galaxies, looking for tiny distortions in their positions and shapes. After seven years of rigorous analysis, the collaboration published their final results in early 2026. “It’s been a real tour de force,” said Ferraro, who isn’t part of DES. “It pushed the analysis to a new level.”

Alongside these measurements, DES also reprocessed a catalog they had compiled of 1,600 recently observed supernovas, establishing the sharpest view yet of the modern universe. “I trust the DES-reanalyzed supernova data much more than I trust any other supernova dataset,” said [Seshadri Nadathur (opens a new tab)](https://seshnadathur.github.io/), a DESI cosmologist.

Cosmologists have now assembled their thickest file on the universe to date. DES merged its map of matter clumping, its supernova catalog, DESI’s galaxy shells, and a CMB image, then checked to see how well Lambda-CDM could still account for the whole cosmic history.

The answer: not very well. In their final report, DES scientists found that their data fit somewhat better with the theory that dark energy is not stable and has slackened in recent eons. In the statistical language of physicists, DES reports a “three-sigma” preference for the new theory. That’s significant enough to make people pay attention, especially since it combines data collected in different ways, but it falls far short of the “five-sigma” confidence physicists need to claim a new discovery.

![Image 5: Photo of the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope with the Dark Energy Camera mounted to it from inside the dome.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Blanco-Telescope-cr.CTIO-NOIRLab-DOE-NSF-AURA-R.-Hahn-Fermi-National-Accelerator-Laboratory-scaled.webp)

The Dark Energy Camera was mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope, famous for its role in the 1998 discovery that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, a process thought to be driven by dark energy.

CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA/R. Hahn (Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory)

Adding to the intrigue, DES found that the mismatch can’t be explained away if, for instance, one of the datasets holds some hidden error. If you assume Lambda-CDM is right, the CMB picture doesn’t quite match the matter maps; the matter maps don’t quite match the supernovas; and the supernovas don’t quite match the CMB picture. There is no single item that you can toss from the file to make everything fit, so no single observation looks fishier than the others.

This suggests that the tension is less likely to be a random artifact — the kind that could easily arise from the merger of millions of observations using different instruments — and is more likely to reflect a clash between the real universe and our understanding of it. “There’s something that doesn’t fit,” Ferraro said. And “we’re trying to figure out what that something is.”

## **Mystery Upon Mystery**

Some theorists are deeply skeptical of the idea that dark energy can change. They already face a major challenge in explaining why the vacuum of space has [the specific energy that it seems to have](https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-the-dark-energy-problem-spawned-the-multiverse-hypothesis-20180312/) — an almost imperceptible amount of oomph filling every cubic kilometer of space. Confirmation that dark energy is also changing would layer on a second major challenge: explaining why that mysteriously tiny amount of energy is evaporating at a mysteriously slow rate.

Some cosmologists wonder if they should tweak other assumptions of Lambda-CDM instead, such as the time at which early stars (and possibly other bright objects) burnt off a hydrogen fog that filled the early universe. Lambda-CDM puts this event at roughly 700 million years after the Big Bang. But if this happened roughly 200 million years earlier, Ferraro and collaborators found in a [2025 analysis (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16932), then Lambda-CDM would fit the cosmological data better. “This number is crucial,” Ferraro said. “However, it’s extremely hard to measure.”

![Image 6: A long white and silver building sits on top of a mountain peak.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Rubin-Observatory-cr.RubinObs_NOIRLab_SLAC_NSF_DOE_AURA_A.-Pizarro-D-scaled.webp)

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, seen here, sits on Cerro Pachón, about six miles from Cerro Tololo, the home of the Dark Energy Survey.

RubinObs/NOIRLab/SLAC/NSF/DOE/AURA/A. Pizarro D

Other theorists are looking into the implications of a changing dark energy, such as the possibility that it could shift in tandem with [the mass of dark matter](https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-dark-dimension-could-link-two-of-the-universes-great-unknowns-20260622/).

For observational cosmologists, the next steps are clear: Keep fattening the dossier on the universe. While DES has ended, DESI will continue collecting data until at least 2028. And on the summit of Cerro Pachón in Chile, the [Vera C. Rubin Observatory](https://www.quantamagazine.org/rubin-tracks-skyscraper-size-asteroids-failed-supernovas-and-interstellar-visitors-20260515/) started its survey operations in 2026.

Rubin is a spiritual successor to DES. It now holds the honor of hosting the world’s [largest digital camera](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-biggest-ever-digital-camera-is-this-cosmologists-magnum-opus-20250711/), and astronomers expect its powerful eye to spot roughly 10 billion — with a “b” — galaxies. DES veterans are already flocking to the Rubin collaboration to help analyze those galaxies, pair by pair, just as they did for DES.

Back in the 1990s, the quickening expansion of the universe became clear from the motions of just a few dozen supernovas. Rubin should find millions more. In a dossier comprised of millions of supernovas and billions of galaxies, an exquisitely detailed cosmic history — and an accounting of the forces that shaped it — will be laid bare for all to see.

![Image 7](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/JOW-S5-E12-cr.Chanelle-Nibbelink-HP-NO-LOGO-1720x729.webp)

# Love Anyway

### By Maria Popova

You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal.

I think about this and a passage from Louise Erdrich’s 2005 novel [**_The Painted Drum_**](https://www.amazon.com/Painted-Drum-Novel-Louise-Erdrich/dp/0060515104/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/71443987)) flits across the sky of my mind:

> Life will break you. Nobody can protect you from that, and living alone won’t either, for solitude will also break you with its yearning. You have to love. You have to feel. It is the reason you are here on earth. You are here to risk your heart. You are here to be swallowed up. And when it happens that you are broken, or betrayed, or left, or hurt, or death brushes near, let yourself sit by an apple tree and listen to the apples falling all around you in heaps, wasting their sweetness. Tell yourself that you tasted as many as you could.

This, of course, is what life evolved to be — an aria of affirmation rising like luminous steam from the cold dark silence of an indifferent cosmos that [will one day swallow all of it](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/16/endling/). Every living thing is its singer and its steward — something the poetic paleontologist Loren Eiseley captures with uncommon poignancy in his 1957 essay “The Judgment of the Birds,” found in his altogether magnificent posthumous collection [**_The Star Thrower_**](https://www.amazon.com/Star-Thrower-Loren-Eiseley/dp/0156849097/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/754773610)).

[![Image 33](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/raven_JackieMorris.jpg?resize=521%2C700&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/06/17/the-lost-words-macfarlane-morris/)

Raven by Jackie Morris from [_The Lost Words_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/06/17/the-lost-words-macfarlane-morris/) by Robert Macfarlane

Eiseley recounts resting beneath a tree after a day of trekking through fern and pine needles collecting fossils, dozing off in the warm sunlight, then being suddenly awakened by a great commotion to see “an enormous raven with a red and squirming nestling in his beak” perching on a crooked branch above. He writes:

> Into the glade fluttered small birds of half a dozen varieties drawn by the anguished outcries of the tiny parents. No one dared to attack the raven. But they cried there in some instinctive common misery, the bereaved and the unbereaved. The glade filled with their soft rustling and their cries. They fluttered as though to point their wings at the murderer. There was a dim intangible ethic he had violated, that they knew. He was a bird of death. And he, the murderer, the black bird at the heart of life, sat on there, glistening in the common light, formidable, unmoving, unperturbed, untouchable. The sighing died. It was then I saw the judgment. It was the judgment of life against death. I will never see it again so forcefully presented. I will never hear it again in notes so tragically prolonged. For in the midst of protest, they forgot the violence. There, in that clearing, the crystal note of a song sparrow lifted hesitantly in the hush. And finally, after painful fluttering, another took the song, and then another, the song passing from one bird to another, doubtfully at first, as though some evil thing were being slowly forgotten. Till suddenly they took heart and sang from many throats joyously together as birds are known to sing. They sang because life is sweet and sunlight beautiful. They sang under the brooding shadow of the raven. In simple truth they had forgotten the raven, for they were the singers of life, and not of death.

Couple with Hannah Arendt on [love and how to live with the fundamental fear of loss](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/02/25/love-and-saint-augustine-hannah-arendt/), then revisit Loren Eiseley on [the warblers and the wonder of being](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/03/loren-eiseley-birds/).

# How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 35: How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/thisday_wendellberry.jpg?fit=320%2C480&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/This-Day-Collected-Sabbath-Poems/dp/1619024365/?tag=braipick-20)

“Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of [her love letters to Susan](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/12/10/emily-dickinson-love-letters-susan-gilbert/) an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a [short and lovely poem](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/01/16/kurt-vonnegut-joe-heller-having-enough/), distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. It is not an easy knowledge to live with amid the commodified counterfeits of happiness that light up these sunset days of Western civilization, with its mesmerism of maximums and its cult of more, materially and spiritually — capitalism goads us to do more in order to own more while the secular church of self-improvement goads us to be more in order to do more.

Against this backdrop, to take a sabbath is a radical act, an act of countercultural courage and resistance, none more radical than a sabbath taken in nature — that eternal pasture of enoughness, which knew from the outset to create just enough more matter than antimatter for the first small seed of something to bloom into everything; which knows daily to make everything, from the electron to the elephant, take up just as much space and energy as it needs to be exactly what it is; which made every life finite and set a limit even to the speed of light.

To be in nature, without doing, is to be reminded [that we are nature, too](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/10/america-ferrera-sojourns-in-the-parallel-world-denise-levertov/); that we cannot force the creative force that made us; that we need not keep breaking our own hearts on expectation’s cold hard edge of not-enough.

[![Image 36](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/thefateoffausto_oliverjeffers2.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/12/06/the-fate-of-fausto-oliver-jeffers/)

Art from [_The Fate of Fausto_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/12/06/the-fate-of-fausto-oliver-jeffers/) by Oliver Jeffers — a modern fable about the existential triumph of enoughness, inspired by Vonnegut

The poet, farmer, and wise elder [Wendell Berry](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/wendell-berry/), who once defined wisdom as [“the art of minimums,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/17/wendell-berry-hidden-wound/) takes up these immense and intimate questions throughout his wonderful collection [**_This Day_**](https://www.amazon.com/This-Day-Collected-Sabbath-Poems/dp/1619024365/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/830371121)) — his series of sabbath poems composed between 1979 and 2013, celebrating the sabbath as a “rich and demanding” idea that “gains in meaning as it is brought out-of-doors and into a place where nature’s principles of self-sustaining wholeness and health are still evident,” a place where “the natural and the supernatural, the heavenly and the earthly, the soul and the body, the wondrous and the ordinary, all appear to occur together in the one fabric of creation.”

In the preface, Berry considers how nature calibrates expectation — even in the creative act itself, where inspiration is not a reach for more but a letting be of what is, a surrender to reality, which is miracle enough:

> On Sunday mornings I often attend a church in which I sometimes sat with my grandfather, in which I sometimes sit with my grandchildren, and in which my wife plays the piano. But I am a bad-weather churchgoer. When the weather is good, sometimes when it is only tolerable, I am drawn to the woods on the local hillsides or along the streams… In such places, on the best of these sabbath days, I experience a lovely freedom from expectations — other people’s and also my own. I go free from the tasks and intentions of my workdays, and so my mind becomes hospitable to unintended thoughts: to what I am very willing to call inspiration. The poems come incidentally or they do not come at all. If the Muse leaves me alone, I leave her alone. To be quiet, even wordless, in a good place is a better gift than poetry.

In how it thrives on the freedom from expectation, in how it demands a total surrender and breaks the moment it is demanded of, creativity has a lot in common with love. It may be that nature invented love to teach us the art of enoughness — to learn how to open the heart to another without condition or expectation, to be fully welcomed in another heart in order to learn the hardest axiom of being: that we are, and always were, enough.

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Yellow-WingedWoodpecker.jpg?resize=680%2C1052&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/07/26/almanac-of-birds/)

Card from [_An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/07/26/almanac-of-birds/)

Love’s salutary alchemy of enoughness comes alive in the second part of Berry’s eight-part sabbath poem of 1994:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iR2U-yJEuxQ)

> Finally will it not be enough,  
>  after much living, after  
>  much love, after much dying  
>  of those you have loved,  
>  to sit on the porch near sundown  
>  with your eyes simply open,  
>  watching the wind shape the clouds  
>  into the shapes of clouds?
> 
> 
> Even then you will remember  
>  the history of love, shaped  
>  in the shapes of flesh, ever-changing  
>  as the clouds that pass, the blessed  
>  yearning of the body for body,  
>  unending light. You will remember, watching  
>  the clouds, the future of love.

Couple with [_John J. Plenty and Fiddler Dan_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/07/29/john-j-plenty-fiddler-dan/) — a lovely vintage illustrated fable about the meaning and measure of enough — then revisit this [soulful animated adaptation](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/12/wendell-berry-the-peace-of-wild-things-animated/) of Berry’s poem “The Peace of Wild Things” and his prose meditation on [the nature of the universe lensed through a sunflower](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/07/01/wendell-berry-sunflower/).
